newsitem.title: USA: Fed rate hike may hinder budget efforts - lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Fed rate hike may hinder budget efforts - lawmakers.

text.p: Lawmakers criticized the Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates on Tuesday, saying more steps to tighten credit could hamper efforts to balance the U.S. budget.

The Fed raised interest rates for the first time in more than two years, pushing short-term rates up a quarter of a percentage point and prompting several banks to raise their benchmark prime lending rates.

The Fed's move by itself was not expected to have an impact on the budget deficit, but lawmakers were concerned that more rate increases could sharply curtail economic growth. That in turn could cut government revenues and also raise interest costs for the U.S. Treasury.

Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, criticized the Fed move. "There's no question that the decision by (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan and the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates will make it harder for Congress and the President to reach a balanced budget," he said.

"A rate increase will likely slow economic expansion, thus reducing the amount of revenues coming into the Federal treasury. This Fed muzzle on the economy will only make an already strained budget process even more difficult," he said.
Republican lawmakers were not as critical of the Fed move, although the members of the leadership did not issue statements. Congress is currently on Spring recess.

Rep. Jim Saxton, chairman of the congressional Joint Economic Committee, said he hoped the rate increase would not lead to follow-up moves. The New Jersey Republican said, "Hopefully this will be all that is undertaken."

And Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican, said: "I'm hopeful that the chairman's (Greenspan's) move will continue to keep inflation under control as well as permit economic growth."
However, one congressional aide warned that if the Fed has erred in raising interest rates, and continues along that path, it could increase the budget deficit.

"If it's a mistake then it creates either a slowdown or an outright recession," the aide said. "It makes the budget deficit bigger and therefore makes the size of the problem of reducing the budget deficit bigger," he said.
An economic slowdown or recession would mean lower tax revenues and higher federal spending for welfare, unemployment insurance and increased borrowing costs.

"At the same time it means that politicians' constituents are hurting and so they're going to be less inclined to do things like cut spending or raise taxes to close the budget deficit," the congressional aide said.
Congressional Republicans and the White House have pledged to try to balance the budget by 2002.
Sen. Paul Sarbanes, a Maryland Democrat member of the Senate Budget Committee, denounced the interest rate increase, but said it was unlikely to affect near-term budget talks.
Sarbanes said the Fed used "bad judgment" in raising rates and called the move "deplorable."
"A growing economy is helpful to reducing the deficit," Sarbanes said. "If you slow the economy down, you lose that benefit."
